title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: an interview, line by line

questions.prompt: In the debate club a pupil takes the floor first, defends her case without a tremble and answers every objection; when the hour is over she shuts her file and talks about other things all evening. Which of these describes her?

options.text: a naïve newcomer
a ruthless rival
a self-confident girl
a debater obsessed with winning

questions.explanation: "a self-confident girl" is right: to be self-confident is to be sure of yourself and of what you can do, and taking the floor first and meeting every objection without a tremble is that assurance in action. "a debater obsessed with winning" is the trap, because an obsessed person can think of nothing else, while this pupil shuts her file and moves on the moment the hour is over. "a naïve newcomer" says the opposite of what she shows, somebody who has not yet learnt how a debate works, and "a ruthless rival" would mean she is cruel to the people she argues with, which nothing here says she is.

questions.prompt: Carol is seventeen and still at school. Why does a national newspaper give her a whole page of interview?

options.text: Because she has agreed to marry her friend Max.
Because she has become a rich star at seventeen.
Because she has just left her all-girls school.
Because she has written a book about pocket money.

questions.explanation: "Because she has become a rich star at seventeen." is the reason: the interest of the story is the gap between her age and the sum the press credits her with. "Because she has just left her all-girls school." is false, since she is still a pupil there. "Because she has written a book about pocket money." invents a book that does not exist, and "Because she has agreed to marry her friend Max." is exactly what the interview denies: she and Max grew up together and are only friends.

questions.prompt: Some newspapers wrote that Carol has already made £20 million. She answers that she is not as rich as the press say. What does her answer tell the reader?

options.text: She says the newspapers' figure is too high.
She will earn twenty million pounds at twenty-one.
She has never earned any money from her records.
She refuses to talk about money in public.

questions.explanation: "She says the newspapers' figure is too high." is right: she does not deny earning money, she corrects the amount, which is what not as rich as they say means. "She has never earned any money from her records." makes her denial total, which her own words do not. "She refuses to talk about money in public." is contradicted by the fact that she answers. The classic trap is "She will earn twenty million pounds at twenty-one.": twenty-one is the age at which she can touch the money, not the age at which she earns it.

questions.prompt: Two sentences use the word publicity. (1) "Since her first record the singer has had to live with publicity." (2) "He turned the sound down because the publicity was too long." Which of these four statements is right?

options.text: (2) is the English use: publicity is what is shown between two films.
(1) and (2) are both English uses, since publicity covers the two ideas.
(1) is the English use: publicity is the money a record brings in each year.
(1) is the English use: publicity is the attention of press and public.

questions.explanation: "(1) is the English use: publicity is the attention of press and public." is right. In English the word names what newspapers, television and people say about somebody, which is why a singer has to live with it once she is known. Sentence (2) uses the word as French does, for what is shown between two programmes: English calls that advertising, never publicity. So the statement that puts the English use on sentence (2) is the trap for a French speaker; the one that turns publicity into the money a record brings in confuses it with income; and the one that says both sentences are English keeps the false friend alive instead of killing it.

questions.prompt: Carol is seventeen. She says that the house she lives in is her own, and that she will have access to her fortune at twenty-one. Which statement about her is true today?

options.text: Her parents own both the house and the whole fortune.
She owns a house but cannot touch her fortune yet.
She owns absolutely nothing at all until she is twenty-one.
She will only buy her house when she is twenty-one.

questions.explanation: "She owns a house but cannot touch her fortune yet." is right: the two facts are separate, and only the money has an age condition on it. "She owns absolutely nothing at all until she is twenty-one." spreads the condition to the house as well, and "She will only buy her house when she is twenty-one." turns a house she already owns into a future purchase. "Her parents own both the house and the whole fortune." is the reading the interview refuses, since Carol says the house is hers.

questions.prompt: Carol replies with five words only: "I'm a mixture of both." Which question had the journalist just asked?

options.text: Do you consider yourself a girl or a young woman?
Has your career made you grow up fast?
Newspapers talk a lot about your looks. What do you think of that?
What's the truth about your relationship with Max?

questions.explanation: "Do you consider yourself a girl or a young woman?" is the one: the word both needs two things named in the question, and only this one offers a choice between two. "Has your career made you grow up fast?" is a yes-or-no question and would be answered with a short answer. "What's the truth about your relationship with Max?" and "Newspapers talk a lot about your looks. What do you think of that?" both name a single topic, so both would leave the word both pointing at nothing.
